ai_summary: Great Britain currently records a total GB wind output of 9.8 GW, supported by an estimated Scottish wind output of 4.0 GW, which constitutes 39.6% of installed Scottish wind capacity. Driven by this robust regional renewable volume, Scottish carbon intensity has dropped to 0 gCO2/kWh, comparing exceptionally well against a GB-wide carbon intensity of 94 gCO2/kWh. Despite this clean generation, transmission infrastructure limitations prevent the full transfer of power across key boundaries to demand centers, resulting in substantial curtailment. Scottish generation curtailed so far today has accumulated to 8895.3 MWh, incurring a constraint cost of about £220,919. To balance the electricity network and satisfy national demand elsewhere, thermal resources must ramp up to fill the deficit created by these transmission bottlenecks. Consequently, the estimated gas burned elsewhere to replace it has reached 1690107.0 m3, which directly produced 3113.4 tonnes CO2 in replacement emissions. This dynamic highlights the operational, fiscal, and ecological frictions present across the power system, where consumers shoulder payments to turn off zero-carbon power while fossil-fueled generators increase output and elevate emissions elsewhere.
